title: Paul Ehrlich, born into a Jewish family, found a way to measure and standardize the serum against diphtheria

trailer.text: Paul Ehrlich was a physician and researcher whose work led to Salvarsan, a syphilis treatment that marked the beginning of the chemotherapeutic era.
Paul Ehrlich, born into a Jewish family, was born in 1854 in Strehlen, Silesia, obtained a doctorate of medicine, and in 1908 shared the Nobel Prize with Metchnikoff.
Emil Behring worked in Berlin on a serum against diphtheria, but his results were inconsistent.
Ehrlich developed a way to measure the effectiveness of serums, and so it became possible to standardize the serum against diphtheria in units related to a fixed standard.
In 1894 Ehrlich, with Kossel and Wassermann, reported on 220 children with diphtheria treated with antitoxin, and in August of that year the company Hoechst began to market the serum.
According to Britannica, his measuring method was soon adopted all over the world.

paragraphs.text: Paul Ehrlich was born on March 14, 1854 in Strehlen, Silesia, Germany.
Strehlen was a town of some 5,000 inhabitants, and today it is in Poland.
He was born into a Jewish family prominent in business and industry.
His cousin was the bacteriologist Carl Weigert, and Weigert was his mentor.
Ehrlich did not convert from Judaism, but he was indifferent to Jewish customs and traditions.
Ehrlich obtained a doctorate of medicine for a dissertation on staining animal tissues.
In 1882 he published his method of staining the tubercle bacillus that Koch had discovered.
In 1888 Ehrlich was infected with the tubercle bacillus in the laboratory, and his scientific career was disrupted.
In 1890 Robert Koch, Director of the new Institute for Infectious Diseases, appointed him as one of his assistants.
In 1892 Ehrlich demonstrated that antibodies are passed in breast milk from mother to newborn.
In another experiment he showed that rabbits given poison in a slow and measured increase survived 5,000 times the fatal dose.

stations.title: The problem: serum of variable quality

paragraphs.text: Until 1893 Emil Behring worked at the Institute of Infectious Diseases in Berlin on a serum against diphtheria and tetanus, but the results were inconsistent.
Serums against diseases were an entirely new type of medicine, and their quality varied greatly.
There were serious quality control problems in the production of antibody serums.
The amount of antitoxin varied greatly from serum to serum.
A standard was therefore needed that would allow it to be measured exactly.
According to Britannica, only a technique of Ehrlich's, which used the blood of live horses, made it possible to prepare a serum of optimum effectiveness against the toxin.
Ehrlich built a standard for von Behring's serum against diphtheria, and the serum could be measured in units related to a fixed standard.
In testing the serum, Ehrlich set a clear target: the test animal was to die after four days.
If it died earlier, the serum was rejected as too weak.
Early in 1894 the clinical tests of the serum were successful, and in August Hoechst began to market it.
That same year Ehrlich, with Kossel and Wassermann, reported on 220 children with diphtheria treated with antitoxin, and stressed the importance of an early, liberal dose.
At the end of 1896 an Institute for the control of therapeutic sera was established at Steglitz in Berlin, and Ehrlich was appointed its Director.
According to Britannica, his measuring method for the standardization of the serum against diphtheria was soon adopted all over the world.

stations.title: The Nobel Prize, seven years later

paragraphs.text: The first Nobel Prize in Medicine was awarded in 1901 for research on diphtheria, and only von Behring received it.
Only seven years later did the Swedish academy recognize the contribution of Ehrlich, who adapted serum therapy to actual medical application.
In 1908 Ehrlich shared the Nobel Prize with Metchnikoff, for their work on immunity.
According to Britannica, Ehrlich's side-chain theory described how antibodies are formed and how they react with other substances.
Even before that, in 1903, Ehrlich received the Prussian Great Gold Medal for Science, which before him had been awarded only to Rudolf Virchow.

stations.title: From the serum to the "magic bullet"

paragraphs.text: Ehrlich knew that serum treatment had limits: many infectious diseases, in particular those caused by protozoa, did not respond to it.
In 1899 the Royal Prussian Institute for Experimental Therapy opened, and Ehrlich directed it until his death.
In 1906 the Georg-Speyer-Haus, a research institute for chemotherapy, was established with an endowment from Franziska Speyer in memory of her husband.
In 1907 Ehrlich and Bertheim synthesized and tested several hundred compounds derived from atoxyl.
Compound number 606 was set aside that year as ineffective.
Hata tested the rejected drug and found that it was very effective.
On 19 April 1910, in Wiesbaden, Ehrlich and Hata reported the discovery of arsphenamine.
It seemed that a "magic bullet" had been found, an expression Ehrlich was fond of.
Salvarsan was the first effective treatment for syphilis, and marked the beginning of the chemotherapeutic era.
It remained the most effective drug for syphilis until penicillin arrived in the 1940s.
Chaim Weizmann, Israel's first President, convinced Ehrlich to serve on the University Committee.
Ehrlich bequeathed money to the Nordau Institute, a forerunner of the Hebrew University.
Ehrlich died in August 1915.
In its obituary the London Times wrote that Ehrlich had opened new doors into the unknown, and that the whole world was in his debt.
According to Encyclopedia.com, Behring overcame the difficulties in antitoxin production with Ehrlich's help, and procured for himself a remunerative contract.
In the end Ehrlich was pressured into accepting only eight percent of the profits.
According to a biography cited by the Forward, Ehrlich's prize was delayed because Arrhenius, a Swedish scientist on the committee, was irked by the "markedly Jewish atmosphere" of the institute.
In 1901 Max von Gruber launched a two-year polemic against the side-chain theory, and the polemic soon became insulting.
After Salvarsan, fanatics and sensationalist commentators accused him of charlatanism, profiteering and ruthless experimentation.
The accusations of excessive enrichment were made with clearly anti-Semitic undertones.
In March 1914 the Reichstag endorsed Salvarsan.
The most libelous of his opponents was given a jail sentence.
Paul Uhlenhuth, an associate of Ehrlich's, claimed that he had discovered the drug first.
In Frankfurt the name of Paul Ehrlich Street was removed because Ehrlich was a Jew.
During the Third Reich his achievements were ignored, and von Behring was presented as the ideal Aryan scientist.
The Nazi government opposed a 1940 film about Ehrlich.
Shortly after the war the name Paul-Ehrlich-Strasse was reinstated, and many German cities named streets after him.

claims.text: עד 1940 שינו הנאצים את שם הרחוב בפרנקפורט שבו שכן מכונו של ארליך, משום שהיה יהודי.
claims.quote: By 1940, the Frankfurt street in which Ehrlich’s Institute had been located, previously Paul Ehrlichstrasse, had been renamed by the Nazis because Ehrlich was Jewish.

claims.text: בתקופת הרייך השלישי הוזנחו הישגי ארליך, ואילו פון בהרינג הוצג כמדען הארי האידיאלי.
claims.quote: During the Third Reich, Ehrlich's achievements were ignored while Emil Adolf von Behring was stylized as the ideal Aryan scientist

claims.text: הממשל הנאצי התנגד להוקרה למדען יהודי בסרט על ארליך מ-1940, ונעשו ניסיונות להסתיר את הסרט בגרמניה.
claims.quote: Since the Nazi government was opposed to this tribute to a Jewish scientist, attempts were made to keep the film a secret in Germany.

claims.text: זמן קצר לאחר המלחמה הוחזר השם פאול-ארליך-שטראסה, וערים גרמניות רבות קראו רחובות על שמו.
claims.quote: Shortly after the end of the war the name Paul-Ehrlich-Strasse was reinstated and today numerous German cities have streets named after Paul Ehrlich.

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה.קום, ארליך היה הבן היחיד והילד הרביעי של אב יהודי שהיה מזקק, בעל פונדק ואוסף הגרלות.
claims.quote: He was the only son and fourth child of Ismar Ehrlich, a respected but somewhat eccentric Jewish distiller, innkeeper, and lottery collector

claims.text: ארליך היה הילד השני של איסמר ורוזה ארליך.
claims.quote: Paul Ehrlich was the second child of Ismar and Rosa Ehrlich.

claims.text: לפי JewishGen, ארליך קיבל את הדוקטורט ב-1882 ואחר כך עבד בשריטה בברלין.
claims.quote: After obtaining his doctorate in 1882, he worked at the Charité in Berlin as an assistant medical director under Theodor Frerichs

claims.text: לפי המאמר בפרמקולוגיה, מכונו של ארליך סיפק 65,000 דגימות חינם לניסויים קליניים נוספים.
claims.quote: Their announcement at this congress led to a large number of requests, which Ehrlich's institute fulfilled by dispensing 65,000 free samples so that further clinical trials could be done.

claims.text: לפי בריטניקה, היצרן פארבוורקה-הואכסט הפיץ 65,000 יחידות חינם לרופאים ברחבי העולם.
claims.quote: the manufacturer with whom Ehrlich had collaborated closely, Farbwerke-Hoechst, released a total of 65,000 units gratis to physicians all over the globe

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה.קום, בית גיאורג שפייר סיפק עד סוף השנה כ-65,000 מנות חינם.
claims.quote: By the year’s end, when the full resources of the Georg-Speyer-Haus had provided about 65,000 doses gratis

claims.text: לפי JewishGen, סלברסן הוחלף בניאוסלברסן ב-1911.
claims.quote: Salvarsan required improvement as to side effects and solubility and was replaced in 1911 with Neosalvarsan.

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה.קום, ניאוסלברסן הוכנס לשימוש קליני ב-1912.
claims.quote: It was introduced for clinical use in 1912 as Neosalvarsan.

claims.text: לפי המאמר בפרמקולוגיה, עבודתו של ארליך זכתה להכרה בעשרה תארי דוקטור לכבוד.
claims.quote: Ehrlich's work was recognized with ten honorary doctorates and the Prussian Great Gold Medal for Science(1903), awarded previously only to Rudolf Virchow.

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה.קום, הוענקו לארליך שנים עשר אותות הוקרה וחמישה תארי דוקטור לכבוד.
claims.quote: Twelve orders (ten from foreign governments) and five honorary doctorates were conferred on him.

sources.label: The Forward, Paul Ehrlich, a 'Markedly Jewish' Humanitarian
